title: VA9-04699
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision in the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "principal claimant"), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "associated claimants") who claim to be citizens of El Salvador and are claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1 DETERMINATION

I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution on a Convention ground in El Salvador. I also find that the claimants are not persons in need of protection in that their removal to El Salvador would not subject them personally to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. I also find that there are no substantial grounds to believe that their removal to El Salvador would subject them personally to a danger of torture. My reasons are as follows: IDENTITY
The claimants' identities and their citizenship as nationals of El Salvador have been established by the testimony and supporting documentation filed and entered in these proceedings.2 ALLEGATIONS
The following is a synopsis of the claimants allegations taken from the Personal Information Form (PIF) of the claimants as supplemented by their testimony and other evidence at the hearing.
The principal claimant and associated claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are brothers, the associated claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is the common law spouse of the principal claimant.

The problems with the Mara Salvatrucha gang started for the brothers before the principal claimant met his common law spouse. In XXXX 2004 the principal claimant was going to the grocery store to get groceries when he was approached by a Mara gang member who asked him for money. He refused to give him any and the gang member started to beat him up.

His brother XXXX, the associated claimant, saw what was happening and went to his brother's aid. They then were surrounded by many gang members who were shouting at them. The gang leader named "XXXX" arrived and asked about what was going on. He then ordered the gang members to stand back and let XXXX and the gang member fight.

Once the gang member realized he was not going to get support from his fellow gang members he no longer wanted to fight XXXX. This ended the confrontation but the gang member was upset with the brothers.

In XXXX 2004 the gang member came to the neighbourhood where the brothers lived. One of his friends took the hat off the head of the principal claimant in order to provoke him. Again XXXX came to the defence of his brother by snatching the hat back. The gang member pulled a gun and pointed it at XXXX telling him if he did not give the hat back he would shoot him. Jamie gave the hat back and that was the end of the altercation.

One evening in the summer of 2004 the brothers were walking together when they were told to stop by two gang members. The brothers did not stop as they did not want a confrontation. One of the two gang members was the same person who they had had the previous encounters with.

They caught up with the brothers and one of the gang members kicked the principal claimant in the back. They demanded that the brothers give them all the money they had or they would cut them. He pulled out a knife.
The brothers did not have any money to give them. XXXX was able to kick the knife out of the hand of the gang member. The brothers then fought the gang members. They won the fight.

After this incident the brothers were afraid for their lives. They did not report any of the incidents to the police because they believe that the police have been infiltrated by the Mara and if they filed a complaint the Mara would find out and they would be in more danger. They also believed that the police would do nothing to help them.
XXXX had a Visa that would allow him to enter the United States. He left El Salvador for the United States in XXXX 2004.

In XXXX 2004 the principal claimant was walking home from the bus stop around ten or eleven at night when he heard some people behind him. When they caught up with him it turned out to be the same gang member with two of his friends. They appeared to be drunk or high on drugs. They asked him for money but he had no money with him. They threatened him saying this was his day and no one was going to help him. They pulled a gun on him, pulled down his pants and beat him. They burned his genitals and ankles with hot coals that had been left on the street by food vendors. They demanded that he get them $1,000.00 in a week or they would kill him. They released him and he went home.
He did not report this incident to the police either for the same reasons as before.
He talked to his brother in the U.S. and told him what had happened and warned him not to come back as they had been targeted by the Mara.
The principal claimant then moved to XXXX before the week was up. It was here that he met XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, the associated claimant, who would later become his common law spouse.

Around the same time XXXX met the principal claimant she was harrassed by a Mara gang member named "XXXX." XXXX would make obscene remarks to her when she would walk by. He would follow her and tell her that someday she would be his girlfriend and that he was going to sleep with her. He would grab her buttocks when he saw her on the street. He told her that he would never leave her in peace until she gave herself to him.
His advances caused a great deal of psychological stress for XXXX. She did not report this to police for the same reason as the brothers did not report their incidents.

XXXX went to New Year celebrations with her father and other family members. She was dancing with her father when XXXX approached her from behind with a knife. He pulled the knife on her and said "your hour has come." He father came to her aid and then other people joined in taking XXXX to the ground. He was taken out by the people that had subdued him but on his way out he was saying that this is not the end of it and that one day he would meet her alone. She filed a report with the police and then she, her father, and the principal claimant moved to her fathers place in XXXX.

The principal claimant suggested that the best thing for them to do was to go to the United States. They did not have enough money for all three of them to travel so she went alone entering the United States illegally in XXXX 2005 where she stayed with her aunt in California.
The principal claimant was able to enter the United States illegally on XXXX, 2005, where he reunited with the associated claimants.
None of the claimants attempted to claim asylum in the United States because they did not know that they could.

All three left the United States for Canada because they could not get status there and they feared immigration would pick them up and send them back to El Salvador. XXXX was also having trouble with a man named XXXX XXXX XXXX stalking her. ANALYSIS Credibility
For the purposes of this analysis I will assume without deciding that the claimants are credible. CLAIMANTS XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX AND XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

For these claimants to be Convention refugees their fear of persecution must be by reason of one of the five grounds enumerated in the Convention refugee definition. In other words, they must have a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.

In this case, the evidence is that the principal claimant and his brother were allegedly targeted by members of a criminal gang known as Mara. They were the subject of extortion on a regular basis. The extortion took the form of the gang member demanding small amounts of money from them when they were on the street. The claimants stated that this is very common in El Salvador. The reason the brothers had problems with the Mara was because the principal claimant refused to give them money and they defended themselves against their attacks.
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the principal claimant and his brother were targeted by criminals for financial gain and for no other reason.
I, therefore, find that the harm feared by the principal claimant and his brother does not fall within one of the five grounds enumerated in the Convention refugee definition.
I find that the principal claimant and his brother are not Convention refugees as defined under section 96 of the Act.

In order to qualify as a person in need of protection under section 97(1)(a) the claimants must be subjected to pain or suffering that is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity.
No allegations of torture under section 97(1)(a) were made and, therefore, I determine that no claim under section 97(1)(a) has been established.

I then examine the evidence as it applies to whether the principal claimant and his brother would face a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment as outlined in section 97(1)(b) of the Act. I will enter into that analysis later in these reasons.

The situation for claimant XXXX is somewhat different in that she is a member of a particular social group, that being women who are targeted for sexual abuse. I will examine her claim under section 96.
The determinative issue for this claimant is internal flight alternative (IFA).

The panel considered whether there is an internal flight alternative in the claimants' country of origin where she could live safely without a serious possibility of being persecuted. The claimant was advised that IFA was an issue before and at the hearing. Case law indicates that the test for an IFA has two parts. First, whether the claimants would be safe from harm in a different part of El Salvador and, second, whether it would not be unreasonable in their particular circumstances to relocate there.3

XXXX was asked if there was a place in El Salvador where she could live in safety. The Panel proposed the city of La Union as such a place. She stated that there was not a place where she could go and live safely. She believed that because of the prevalence of Mara gangs in El Salvador and her belief that they all communicate with each other that XXXX would be able to locate her no matter where she went.

XXXX was asked if she was satisfied that XXXX would not find her would she be able to re-locate within El Salvador to which she responded that she would have considered it but that she is also concerned about the high crime rate anywhere in El Salvador due to the prevalence of gangs.

Her evidence is that she was approached by Mara gang members on many occasions and forced to give them, usually small amounts of money, out of fear of being injured. She stated that she was in no better or worse position in this regard that the majority of her fellow citizens. Then in 2004, shortly after she and the principal claimant started dating, one particular Mara gang member named XXXX started to make comments with sexual overtones to her.

He stated that she was going to be his girl and he would grab her buttocks on several occasions when he saw her on the street. She did not report this incident to the police because she was afraid that the police co-operated with the Mara and he would find out she had gone to the police and that would make matters worse for her.

On News Year Eve 2004 XXXX was with her father at a celebration put on by the town. While XXXX was dancing with her father, XXXX came up to her from behind and put a knife to her chest. Her father and others intervened, overpowered him and took him out. He threatened her life as he was being taken away. No one called the police on this occasion either. She made a report to the police the next day but feels that the police did nothing about her complaint.

She stated that she had known who XXXX was for some time because XXXX is a small town and he is a well know gang member but that he did not start bothering her with sexually charged harassment until after she started dating the principal claimant. She stated that he is still in XXXX.

The claimants stated they believed that all Mara gangs have a network and can communicate with each other. The principal claimant and XXXX both stated that the fact that XXXX did not have any problems with XXXX beyond small time extortion before they started dating proves that the gangs communicate. They stated that they believed XXXX was being singled out for this type of harassment by XXXX because of the problems the principal claimant had with the Mara in his home town of XXXX.

Although the principal claimant and XXXX may subjectively believe that the gangs have an efficient communications network and/or reciprocal enforcement strategies the evidence suggests something different.

Country documents tell that there are approximately twenty five thousand street gang members with ten to thirteen and a half being members of the Mara XX or XX.4 This means that approximately half of the street gang members are not Mara.

The principal claimant testified that he was told that if he did not give them one thousand dollars in one week they were going to kill him. If the Mara gang that targeted him was associated to the gang in XXXX then it is logical that they would have followed through with their threat or at the very least directly contacted the principal claimant to continue their extortion of him. There is no evidence that they took any further action to follow through on their threat.

XXXX and the principal claimant assumed that XXXX sexual interest in her was connected to the problems that the principal claimant had with the Mara gang in his home of XXXX but there is no objective evidence to support this assumption. There is also no evidence that XXXX made any reference to the principal claimant or his problems with the gang in XXXX during his approaches to XXXX.

The evidence is that the extortionists demanded as little as fifty cents to one dollar from their victims. This does not suggest a sophisticated criminal organization but rather one that is of a much lower level.

The claimants stated that they identified their tormentors as Mara by their tattoos but their low level criminal activity such as stealing a hat and extorting as little as fifty cents does not suggest that they have ties to organized crime.

I find based on the evidence before me that XXXX and/or the Mara organization he belongs to, if he is a Mara member, are not sophisticated enough to have the capacity to locate XXXX should she relocate to La Union.

I find that there is no serious possibility that the associated claimant XXXX would be persecuted, or that she would be subjected on a balance of probabilities to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in La Union.
The next consideration is whether it would be unreasonable in her particular circumstances to relocate there.5

XXXX is a young woman who was able to leave El Salvador and establish herself in the United States for several years. When she became concerned with lack of employment opportunities and that American Immigration officials were stepping up enforcement she was able to make her way to Canada. She has now established herself here.

She has demonstrated a significant capacity to adapt and adjust. She is a citizen of El Salvador and would have no language issues in the IFA. She would have family support should she return to her home country. There would be as many employment opportunities in La Union as any other similarly sized city in El Salvador.

XXXX has expressed her concern about the general crime situation in her country including any IFA. Although I empathize with her in this regard the general rate of crime in a specific area does not render it an unfit IFA.
I find that an IFA does exist for associated claimant XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Whether this claim is framed under section 96 or 97 there is an internal flight alternative available to the claimant. I therefore deny the claim of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX under section 96 and 97 of the Act.
I will now deal with the remaining two claimants.

A person in need of protection must show that the removal to the country of reference would subject them personally to the harm feared. The fact that documentary evidence shows systemic and generalized human rights violations is in no way sufficient to establish a specific individualized fear of persecution with regard to the claimants in particular.
The claimant must demonstrate that he would be personally in danger of risk having regard to his own circumstances and those of similarly situated persons.
Section 97(1)(ii) states that: The risk would be faced by the person in every part of the country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country.

Country documents tell me that violence is a problem in El Salvador. The United States Department of State Report states that: The protection of human rights was undermined by widespread violent crime including gang-related violence. Several sources indicate that El Salvador is one of the most dangerous countries in the world. Fear of violence even causes some individuals to limit their movement and participation in certain events. Today El Salvador has hundreds of known street gangs totalling more than 30,000 members. The government is taking steps to dismantle street gangs; however, several sources confirm that these strategies have not improved public safety.6
This is consistent with the testimony of the claimants, who stated that gangs regularly and routinely extort money from citizens by threatening them with violence.
The evidence in this claim is that the brothers were approached by Mara gang members for money just like many other El Salvadorian citizens.

They testified that the Mara gangs work in a geographical area in small groups with each group having a leader. They were targeted by a specific Mara gang group when the principal claimant refused to give them money they had demanded.
They went on to say that many people are targeted by these gangs and are subjected to violence if they do not comply.

I can understand why these claimants would be concerned regarding the alleged criminal attacks they have endured. The evidence is that the principal claimant and his brother were the victims of crime but the crime they were subjected to is faced generally by much of the population of El Salvador. I find that the crime these two claimants were victims of is faced generally by other citizens of El Salvador and as a result are not persons in need of protection as defined in section 97(1)(b) of the Act.
Having considered all the evidence I find that the principal claimant and his brother are not persons in need of protection as defined under section 97 of the Act.
I therefore reject their claims under section 96 and 97 of the Act.

Having considered all the evidence I find that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are not Convention Refugees or persons in need of protection and I therefore reject their claims. (signed) "Gordon C.
